pages.text:
*Days without rain: 117. Buckets from the spring: 10.*

That evening, the courtyard behind Yeye Gu’s house filled with people. There was no room to sit, so most stood, and a few perched on the low stone wall that held in the garden soil. Yeye Gu lit a single oil lamp. The flame caught the smoke from the cooking fires and turned it into a grey swirl.

"Before the paved road," Yeye Gu began, his voice low, "we did not ask the sky. We wrote to a neighbor."

Tao, who had been trying to balance a grain of rice on his tongue, dropped it. "A neighbor?"

"High up," Yeye Gu said, pointing a finger toward the darkening peak. "At Black Pool. He is not a king. He is a river dragon. Small enough to be shy."

Mei looked at the others. The adults were still. The air smelled of woodsmoke and the damp earth that was trying to hold on to the last of its moisture.

"How small?" Tao asked, his voice loud and curious.

Yeye Gu smiled. It was a thin smile, like a crack in dry clay. "Small enough to apologize to a rock if he bumps into it."
pages.image: A crowded stone courtyard at dusk where villagers stand listening to Yeye Gu, an old man with long white eyebrows and a brown vest, who points toward a dark mountain peak while Tao, a gap-toothed boy in yellow boots, leans forward with wide eyes.

pages.text:
"He lives in the mist," Yeye Gu continued, his voice dropping as if he were sharing a secret. "The mist is his coat. And every spring, when the tea buds were just opening, we sent a gift."

He held up a small, dry leaf, turning it so the light caught its veins. "First tea. And a message."

"What message?" asked a woman in the front row.

Yeye Gu’s eyes were bright in the lamplight. "We are here. We are grateful. Please come again."

The courtyard settled into a silence so complete that even the crickets seemed to pause their singing to listen.

"And the rain?" asked Uncle Shi, his thermos clutched tightly in his hands.

"Always came," Yeye Gu said. "Late at night. It rolled down the mountain like a drum, and by morning, the mud was soft and the seeds were drinking." He paused, looking around the circle of faces. "One child carried it. Just one. Over the bridge, up the Cloud Ladder. A simple task. If you knew the way."

Mei felt a small tug in her stomach, a feeling like a balloon string pulling tight. One child. That was not a crowd. That was just one person, walking a path that she had only ever seen from the bottom, where the steps disappeared into the dark.
pages.image: Yeye Gu holding up a single dry tea leaf in the warm glow of an oil lamp, surrounded by a semicircle of attentive villagers, with a dark, misty mountain looming in the background behind them.

pages.text:
"Then why did it stop?" Mei asked. She did not know why she had spoken. The words were out before her mouth could catch them.

Yeye Gu looked at her. He did not seem surprised. "Nobody remembers the year," he said. "Maybe it was when the road was paved. Maybe it was when the young ones went to the cities."

He shrugged, a small movement of his shoulders. "We forgot to say we are here."

The thought hung in the air, heavy and strange. Mei looked at her hands. She had never sent a message. She had never asked anyone to come back.

"So perhaps," Yeye Gu added, his voice dropping to a whisper, "he thinks we are gone."

Tao shifted his weight. "If he thinks we are gone, why would he send rain?"

Yeye Gu did not answer. He simply turned his head and looked at the black shape of the mountain again. The mist was still there, curling and moving, waiting for something it did not have.
pages.image: Mei standing in the courtyard with her hands clasped tightly in front of her, looking at Yeye Gu who is turning his head toward the misty mountain, while Tao looks confused and worried in his yellow boots.

pages.text:
Uncle Shi stepped forward, holding his steel thermos with both hands as if it were the only solid thing left in the world. "Stories do not fill buckets," he said, his voice firm but his eyes heavy with fatigue. "I have written to the county. I asked for water trucks."

Auntie Fen stood by the wall, her purple apron dark in the dim light. "The road is washed out," she said. "The trucks cannot come."

"Then we wait," Uncle Shi replied. "We wait for the water to find us."

"It is not a story about rain," Yeye Gu said softly, without raising his voice. "It is a story about being remembered."

Half the courtyard nodded slowly while the other half frowned, looking first at the dry terraces and then at their own empty hands. Mei felt her thumb press into her palm again, the skin raw now, and it did not hurt so much as it felt like a promise she had made to herself.
pages.image: Uncle Shi in his grey jacket and blue cap holding a steel thermos, standing opposite Auntie Fen in a purple apron, with Yeye Gu looking calmly at the mountain in the background while villagers look divided between frowning and nodding.

pages.text:
A silence fell over the courtyard. It was the heavy, waiting kind, the sort that sits on your shoulders like a wet school backpack.

Then, from the back of the crowd, a small voice spoke.

"I know the path."

Everyone turned. Nainai was sitting on her low stool. She was small and straight-backed, her grey hair pinned in a bun. She did not look up. She looked at her hands.

"I climbed it as a girl," she said. "My knees would not manage the first hill now."

Mei stood in the shadows beside her, her thumb pressed hard into the soft skin of her palm. The air in the courtyard felt thick, like water about to freeze.

Nainai’s voice was quiet. "The path is old. It is still there."

Mei looked at her grandmother, then at the mountain. The mist was swirling around the peak, a soft, white scarf against the dark rock. She wanted to say something. Her mouth opened, but no sound came out.
pages.image: Nainai sitting on a small wooden stool in the back of the courtyard, looking down at her hands, while Mei stands in the shadows beside her, staring at the misty mountain peak with wide eyes.
